\{x:|x-{x}_{0}|<\delta \}

![](images/50/50a6c72e169f3104eb0b9958673cc6644f770e6bcc3ebf23360eb20189325a28.png)

- A point ${x}_{0}$ is an *interior point* of a set $S$ if $S$ contains *some* neighborhood of ${x}_{0}.$ The set of all interior points of $S$ is called the *interior* of $S.$

- A point ${x}_{0}$ is a *boundary point* of a set $S$ if *every* neighborhood of ${x}_{0}$ contains points that are in $S$ and points that are not in $S.$ 
The set of all boundary points of $S$ is called the *boundary* of $S.$

Now, the set $A$ consists of all points that lie below the line $y=1-2x.$ A sketch of this region is shown below:

![](images/7c/7ce1ca6af3caf2b454d7fed484f98d11478839bcf107c0f19562688c7cdaca6a.png)

![](images/aa/aad8bc7bfd64af0dd1e08618626ae3237bb4aba42be1f91fe7ff9328ad6ecbe7.png)

- Statement III is false. The point $Q$ is *not* an interior point of $A$ since any neighborhood of $Q$ contains at least one point *outside* the set.
